scenes.narration: One DNA molecule becomes more than a billion copies in just thirty cycles.
scenes.title: A BILLION COPIES BEFORE LUNCH

scenes.narration: Every cycle has three steps, and each step is just a temperature. At 95 degrees Celsius, the double helix unzips into single strands.
scenes.caption: 3 STEPS

scenes.narration: At about 55 degrees, short primers latch onto their matching sequences. At 72 degrees, a polymerase builds a new strand from each one.
Each cycle doubles the DNA, so thirty cycles give about 1.07 billion copies.
scenes.caption: 2³⁰

scenes.narration: Normal enzymes die at 95 degrees, so early PCR re-added enzyme each cycle.
scenes.caption: ENZYME DIES
scenes.sub: heat-labile Klenow fragment · refilled every cycle

scenes.narration: In 1969, Thomas Brock described Thermus aquaticus, a microbe from Yellowstone hot springs. Its enzyme, Taq polymerase, survives the heat, so the machine only changes temperature.
Kary Mullis conceived PCR in 1983, and won the Nobel Prize in 1993.
Real reactions fall short of perfect doubling, so a billion is a ceiling.
scenes.caption: A CEILING
scenes.sub: real efficiency is below 100% and reagents run out

scenes.narration: Modern genetics leans on an enzyme from a Yellowstone hot spring. Follow for more.

sources.claim: PCR cycle: denaturation ~94-96 C, annealing ~45-60 C (55 C typical), extension ~72 C (Taq optimum); the DNA doubles each cycle; runs of 25-40 cycles.

Arithmetic: 2^30 = 1,073,741,824 (about 1.07 billion); yield is (1+E)^n so real efficiency below 100% gives fewer copies, and reactions plateau when reagents are depleted.
Early PCR used the heat-labile Klenow fragment, inactivated by the heating step; Taq's heat stability meant only temperature changes were required.
